nameStory: New England ragwort gets its name from its range concentrated in northeastern North America, though it's also called New England groundsel. The 'ragwort' part comes from the old English word for the ragged, deeply-cut leaves that many plants in this group display, though this species actually has smoother leaf edges than its relatives.
description: New England ragwort is a cheerful perennial wildflower that brightens wet meadows and sunny bog edges with clusters of bright yellow, daisy-like blooms. Growing up to about 2 feet tall, this member of the sunflower family sends up sturdy stems crowned with multiple flower heads from late spring through midsummer. Its distinctive lance-shaped basal leaves help set it apart from other yellow wildflowers, and it sometimes spreads by underground stems to form small colonies.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Basal leaves are distinctively long and narrow - lance-shaped to triangular and more than 3 times longer than they are wide. They feel smooth to the touch and have a fresh, slightly bitter smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flower heads arranged in flat-topped clusters, each about the size of a quarter. The ray petals (the 'daisy petals') surround a center of tiny disc flowers that feel slightly fuzzy when touched.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows 1-3 feet tall with a rosette of basal leaves and one or more upright flowering stems. Often forms small patches through underground rhizomes that feel firm and fibrous when exposed.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy, upright stems that feel smooth and slightly ridged. They're typically green to reddish-purple and hold their flower clusters well above the basal leaves.

habitat: Look for New England ragwort in sunny, consistently moist areas with acidic soil - think wet meadows, bog edges, marshy spots, and seepage areas in open woods. In New England, it particularly favors the edges of sphagnum bogs and wet openings in coniferous forests. It needs both sunshine and wet feet, so you won't find it in dry uplands or deep shade.

seasonality.spring: Fresh basal leaves emerge early, forming distinctive rosettes with their characteristic long, narrow shape. Flower buds begin developing on emerging stems by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period from May through July, when the bright yellow flower clusters are most showy and easiest to spot. Seeds begin developing in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and fluffy white seed heads develop, dispersing on the wind. Basal leaves may persist but become less prominent.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to underground parts, leaving little trace above ground. Look for dried stems and seed heads in protected areas.

funFact: Despite being called 'New England' ragwort, this plant has a secret southern hideout - it mysteriously pops up on a few high-elevation Appalachian balds in North Carolina and Tennessee, over 1,000 miles from its main northeastern range, likely a remnant from when cooler climates extended much further south during the ice ages.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with golden ragwort, but New England ragwort's basal leaves are the giveaway - they're much longer and narrower (more than 3 times as long as wide) compared to golden ragwort's heart-shaped or rounded basal leaves. Remember: 'New England = Narrow leaves.'
contextualKnowledge: Like other members of the ragwort genus, this plant contains alkaloids that can be toxic to livestock if eaten in large quantities, though it's rarely a problem in the wild wetland habitats where it grows. The name 'groundsel' comes from Old English meaning 'ground swallower,' referring to how these plants can spread and cover ground.
compareHints: New England ragwort stands out among its Packera relatives by its distinctively narrow, lance-shaped basal leaves - golden ragwort has heart-shaped leaves, roundleaf ragwort has round to oval leaves, and butterweed has more deeply lobed leaves. The long, narrow basal leaves that are more than three times longer than wide are the key field mark that separates this species from all its cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Golden ragwort stands out from its ragwort relatives by its distinctive heart-shaped basal leaves - roundleaf ragwort has more rounded leaves, while New England ragwort has more deeply cut basal leaves.

Among its ragwort relatives, roundleaf ragwort is distinguished by its truly spoon-shaped basal leaves - golden ragwort has heart-shaped leaves, while New England ragwort has more oval leaves that taper to both ends.
Among New England's ragworts, balsam ragwort is distinguished by its preference for consistently wet habitats and its more irregularly divided, raggedy-looking leaves.
Among its ragwort relatives, butterweed stands out for its deeply divided, cress-like leaves - golden ragwort has heart-shaped basal leaves, while roundleaf ragwort has rounded, less-divided foliage.
